name: Sargon
source_summary: The historical king of Assyria (Sargon II) whose military campaign against the Philistine city of Ashdod, led by his commander, provides the setting for Isaiah's three-year sign-act of walking barefoot and half-clothed as a warning to Judah.
family_friendly_summary: Sargon was a real, powerful king of Assyria, one of the ancient world's mightiest empires. The Bible mentions him once, when he sent one of his generals to attack and capture the Philistine city of Ashdod. Around that same time, God told the prophet Isaiah to do something unusual and uncomfortable: walk around barefoot and without his outer clothing for three years, as a living warning of what would happen to nations that trusted Egypt instead of trusting God. Sargon's brief mention in the Bible reminds us that God's word to His prophets was spoken into real history, real politics, and real events.
adult_story: Sargon, king of Assyria, is named just once in Scripture, dating the events of Isaiah 20: "In the year that the commander came to Ashdod, when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him, and he fought against Ashdod and captured it" (Isaiah 20:1). Sargon II (reigned c. 722-705 BC) was a genuine, historically attested Assyrian emperor, founder of a new royal line, whose westward campaigns brought Assyrian power crashing against the small kingdoms of the Levant, including the Philistine cities. His capture of Ashdod supplies the historical occasion for one of Isaiah's most striking prophetic sign-acts: God commanded Isaiah to strip off his sackcloth and sandals and walk "naked and barefoot" for three years as a living picture of how Assyria would soon lead away captive Egyptians and Cushites in the same humiliating condition (20:2-4). The point was aimed squarely at Judah: nations tempted to put their hope in Egypt's power rather than the LORD would share Egypt's coming disgrace (20:5-6). Sargon's single appearance grounds prophecy in verifiable geopolitical history rather than vague generality.

devotionals: Sargon's conquest of Ashdod set the moment for Isaiah's warning against trusting Egypt instead of God. May we trust Jesus, not human power, to keep us safe.
